To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Mice prefer to harvest Setaria spp. for food, 2) Mice prefer Amaranthus spp., Setaria spp. and Chenopolodium spp. for mound building and 3) Mice prefer Setaria spp., Amaranthus spp and Chenopolodium for food when availability is taken into consideration.

(i) food preference and food choice in terms of hoarding are not necessarily congruent; (ii) the preference for Setaria as a food item is due to its high lipid content, whereas its use in mound building is due to its large size and high handling time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interrelationship of food choice, seed size, seed handling time and predation risk and their influence on plant selection.
the question of whether the food choice of hoarding animals is based on the food preference or whether the food choice is a compromise that considers handling time as well.
the relationship between food preference and food choice in a context where the food is not eaten but stored in above-ground mounds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mice prefer the most caloric seeds as food and the most abundant ones as building material.
the food preference of M. spicileguris is influenced by the availability and size of the seeds, and the handling time.

the preference for a particular seed species for food is not necessarily the same as the preference for the same seed species for storage material, but that there are some similarities between the preferences for food and storage material, and that handling time and seed characteristics play a role.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mice prefer Setaria as food due to its high caloric content, whereas Amaranthus and Chenopodium are preferred as building material due to their high handling efficiency.
mice prefer Setaria as food, but they prefer to harvest and hoard Amaranthus and Chenopodium seeds.
mice harvest and transport the most abundant species, but prefer to feed on the species with the highest caloric value.
The main takeaway from our work is that
food choice in hoarding animals is not necessarily based on intrinsic features of the seed type but may depend on other factors like predation risk and handling time.
food preferences of hoarding animals do not always reflect their preferences for building material.
food choice in relation to hoarding behaviour is more complex than in relation to feeding behaviour.
